Dutch Transportation & Logistics Sector Faces Credit Freeze, Forcing Layoffs and Service Cuts

A sudden credit freeze has swept through the Dutch Transportation & Logistics industry, leaving many firms struggling to meet their financial obligations and triggering a wave of layoffs and site closures across the country. The crisis, which began earlier this month, has rapidly escalated as lenders have tightened access to working capital, halting new financing for transport operators and logistics providers.

Several regional hubs, including those in Rotterdam, Venlo, and Groningen, have reported significant disruptions as companies slash their operations. At the sprawling EuroTrans BV depot near Rotterdam, dozens of trucks stood idle on Monday, their drivers sent home indefinitely. “We’ve had to cut our scheduled runs by nearly half,” said Annelies de Groot, operations manager at EuroTrans BV. “With no short-term credit available, we simply can’t afford to keep the fleet running at full capacity.”

The Dutch Association of Logistics Employers (DAVL) estimates that over 6,500 jobs have been lost nationwide since the start of the crisis, with further cuts expected in the coming days. “Without access to credit, even firms with strong order books are collapsing under the weight of payroll and fuel costs,” said DAVL spokesperson Maarten Koenders. “We are bracing for a much larger wave of layoffs if financial conditions do not improve quickly.”

Mid-sized firms have been particularly hard hit, as many rely on short-term loans to bridge the gap between invoice payments and operating expenses. “We’ve never seen payments delayed like this, or banks refusing to roll over credit lines,” said Lianne van der Meer, director of the logistics firm NoordCargo. NoordCargo has already suspended activity at its Almere distribution centre and placed 120 workers on temporary leave.

Industry analysts say the crisis has also forced companies to renegotiate leases for depots, consolidate routes, and freeze investment in new vehicles and technology. “The uncertainty is making it impossible for companies to plan even a few weeks ahead,” said Jaap Smits, a transport sector analyst at the consulting group LogiStat.

Union leaders have called for urgent government support, warning that the sector risks permanent damage if the credit freeze persists. “We need immediate relief to protect jobs and keep essential services running,” said FNV union official Saskia van Loon.

As the crisis continues, workers and managers alike are anxiously awaiting signs of financial stabilization. For now, the prospect of further layoffs and service cuts looms large over the Dutch Transportation & Logistics industry.
